summary: This document defines TEAP version 1, a tunnel-based EAP method. It uses TLS to set up a mutually authenticated tunnel between a peer and a server, and carries TLV objects inside the tunnel. It was later replaced by RFC 9930.

eli5.summary: First you build a private tunnel to a gatekeeper, then you pass your proof of identity inside it where no one can see. It has since been replaced by RFC 9930.

subtitle: A standards-track EAP method that builds a TLS tunnel first, then does the real authentication inside it.

tldr.problem: Existing TLS-based tunnel EAP methods were vendor-specific or informational, and the industry wanted a Standards Track tunnel-based EAP method that meets the requirements of RFC 6678.
tldr.mechanism: TEAP runs a TLS handshake in Phase 1 to build a protected tunnel, then in Phase 2 carries TLV objects through it for inner EAP methods, passwords, results and other data, with a cryptographic binding tying the two phases together.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7170 has been obsoleted by RFC 9930 and updated by RFC 9427.

today: RFC 7170 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9930 and updated by RFC 9427. Use the newer RFC for the current definition of TEAP.

sections.title: Why a Standard Tunnel Method
sections.content:
A tunnel-based EAP method sets up a secure tunnel and then runs other EAP methods inside it. Earlier TLS-based examples are PEAP, EAP-TTLS (RFC 5281) and EAP-FAST (RFC 4851), but they were vendor-specific or informational. RFC 6678 lists requirements for a standard method.

TEAP version 1 is based on EAP-FAST, which the EMU working group adopted as the basis, with minor changes to meet those requirements. TEAP packets are carried inside EAP, which runs over carriers such as EAP over LAN, RADIUS or Diameter, and TEAP in turn encapsulates TLS and then TLV objects.
sections.eli5: Earlier secret-handshake systems each belonged to one company. This one is written down as a shared standard so everyone can use the same handshake.

sections.title: The Two Phases and the Layers
sections.content:
After the initial EAP Identity exchange, TEAP has two phases. In Phase 1 a TLS handshake gives an authenticated key exchange and a protected tunnel. The TLS version MUST be 1.2 or later. Implementations MUST support TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA and TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, and ciphersuites without confidentiality MUST NOT be used.

In Phase 2 the peer and server exchange TLVs inside the tunnel to carry out inner authentication, results and extras like channel binding. Phase 2 occurs even if both sides authenticated in Phase 1, and MUST NOT occur if the Phase 1 handshake fails. It MUST always end with a Crypto-Binding TLV exchange and a protected termination exchange.

Four logical entities take part: the peer, the authenticator, the TEAP server and the inner method server. They may be separate or combined. Optional Outer TLVs sit outside the tunnel and are allowed only in the first two messages.
sections.eli5: Step one builds the locked tunnel. Step two is the actual identity check inside it, and it finishes with a final seal that proves nobody swapped places on the way.

sections.title: How a Conversation Runs
sections.content:
The server starts with a TEAP/Start packet that has the S bit set, carries the version and an Authority-ID TLV, and has an empty TLS payload. The version is negotiated: the server offers its highest version, and the peer answers with that version or its own highest lower one. Because the version is not protected by TLS, it is checked again later in the Crypto-Binding TLV.

Sessions can be resumed in two ways. One uses server-side state (cached Session ID, master secret and ciphersuite). The other uses a ticket called a Protected Access Credential (PAC), based on the TLS SessionTicket extension. A Tunnel PAC consists of a PAC-Key (at minimum 48 octets, used as the TLS master secret), a PAC-Opaque (the ticket only the server can read) and an optional PAC-Info. If resumption fails the server can fall back to a full handshake.

Inside Phase 2, inner EAP methods run one after another, never in parallel, carried in EAP-Payload TLVs. After each one the server sends an Intermediate-Result TLV, accompanied by a Crypto-Binding TLV on success. Passwords can be sent with the Basic-Password-Auth-Req and Resp TLVs. At the end a Result TLV exchange closes the tunnel, and peers MUST NOT accept a cleartext EAP Success or Failure before protected result indication is reached.

A peer that is unhappy with a success result can ask for more using the Request-Action TLV. Peer services such as PAC provisioning, certificate provisioning and channel binding need the peer to have authenticated the server first.
sections.eli5: The gatekeeper says hello, you agree on how to talk, build the tunnel, and then show one or more IDs one at a time. A saved ticket lets you skip some steps next time.

sections.title: TEAP Packets and TLVs
sections.content:
A TEAP packet has Code (1 Request, 2 Response), Identifier, Length, Type (55 for TEAP), Flags, a 3-bit Ver field (001 for version 1), and optional Message Length, Outer TLV Length, TLS data and Outer TLVs. The flags are L (length included), M (more fragments), S (start), O (outer TLV length included) and R (reserved).

Everything in Phase 2 is a TLV: an M (mandatory) bit, a reserved bit, a 14-bit type, a 2-octet length and a value. If a mandatory TLV is not supported, the receiver MUST send a NAK TLV and ignore the others. Optional unsupported TLVs can be ignored. Types 1 to 17 are allocated, including Authority-ID, Result, Error, Crypto-Binding, EAP-Payload and PAC.

TEAP does its own fragmentation, because a TLS certificate message can in principle reach 16 MB. The L flag marks the first fragment, M marks all but the last, and the receiver acknowledges each fragment with an empty response.
sections.eli5: Every message is a labeled envelope with small labeled notes inside. A flag on a note says 'you must understand this one', and large messages are sent in pieces with a receipt for each piece.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Crypto-Binding
sections.content:
TEAP uses the PRF and MAC negotiated in TLS. It exports a 40-octet session_key_seed from TLS using the label EXPORTER: teap session key seed and no context data. After each successful inner EAP method, an Intermediate Compound Key (IMCK) is recalculated, mixing the seed with that method's session key, which is taken from the EMSK when the method exports one and from the MSK otherwise.

The Crypto-Binding TLV carries a Compound MAC over the TLV itself, the EAP type, and the Outer TLVs from both first messages. This proves that the tunnel endpoints are the same as the inner method endpoints, and it also verifies the negotiated version. When both EMSK and MSK are possible, rules prevent a downgrade to the weaker MSK-based MAC unless the sender's policy accepts it.

The final MSK and EMSK, 64 octets each, are derived from the last S-IMCK. If no inner method succeeded, they come directly from the session_key_seed.
sections.eli5: Both sides stir secrets from the tunnel and from each ID check into one final key, then sign a note with it. If a sneaky third party was in the middle, the signatures would not match.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TEAP is designed with wireless media in mind, where anyone can capture traffic. Its protection comes from TLS: confidentiality and integrity for the tunnel, plus the Crypto-Binding TLV for the inner methods. The protected Result TLV conveys the real outcome, and the peer SHOULD silently discard a cleartext EAP Success or Failure that does not match it.

The listed benefits include user identity protection, protected inner method negotiation, sequencing of EAP methods, acknowledged success or failure, faster re-authentication through resumption, and mitigation of dictionary and man-in-the-middle attacks. Denial of service by sending erroneous traffic remains possible. The initial identity exchange is in cleartext, so it may carry only an anonymous identity with realm information.

Separating the Phase 1 server from the Phase 2 server is NOT RECOMMENDED, as it risks loss of identity protection, offline dictionary attacks and man-in-the-middle attacks. Peers must authenticate the server before using services such as PAC and certificate provisioning.
sections.eli5: The tunnel keeps eavesdroppers out and the final seal catches impostors. Still, someone can jam the road, and the first hello is said out loud.
